newsitem.title: INDIA: India tea industry worried by separatists' threats.
newsitem.headline: India tea industry worried by separatists' threats.

text.p: Tea industry officials in the troubled northeastern Indian state of Assam said on Tuesday they were constantly under threat from separatist groups and often had to pay extortion money for survival.
"It has always been risky for us to travel in the garden areas because there is much extortion and attacks," said Kamal Chandra Das, a tea broker in Guwahati, the state's biggest city.
Assam has more than 800 tea gardens spread over 450,000 acres (180,000 hectares), providing employment to about 700,000 workers. About 65 percent of India's tea is grown in Assam.
The heavily wooded state of Assam, which borders Bhutan, Bangladesh and Burma, has for decades been rocked by violent secessionist campaigns.
Traders said the guerrillas demand about 2,000 rupees ($56) per hectare as extortion money from tea garden owners and trade officials. They are threatened with death unless the amount is paid.
"They demand a lot of money even from the small gardens, paying which is really difficult," Das said.
Traders said a rise in rebel activities had created fear among traders and growers, but production in the region was not affected.
"All I can say is that production has never been hampered by the political unrest in Assam," Das said. "Production is going on as one can't store the leaves. They have to be immediately processed."
"Movement of produce is also not affected," said one trader. "But there is always fear."

The All Assam Students Union (AASU) has demanded that all tea companies with gardens in Assam contribute 0.50 rupee per kg to set up educational facilities and help provide employment to the local youths.
Several separatist groups are fighting for independent homelands in the northeastern region.
Last week, a tribal guerrilla group involved in recent bombings threatened more violence unless the government called for talks to meet its demand for a separate homeland.
Bodo tribal guerrillas belonging to the Bodo Security Force, which often targets Moslem immigrants and other settlers from the plains, are fighting for a separate homeland within the state.

The outlawed United Liberation Front of Assam has been spearheading a separatist movement since the 1980s, saying immigrants are exploiting Assam's wealth of tea and oil, and that New Delhi has neglected the region's development. ($1=35.7 rupees)
